life_story.short: I grew up in Madurai in a middle-class family, and I always wanted to be independent. I started my career later than most people, first in a non-IT coordination job in Dubai, then I came back to India, studied AI and machine learning online, and moved into software. Today I build production software systems, and I'm working to become an AI engineer. I see everything as an opportunity.
detail: I grew up in Madurai, Tamil Nadu, in a small middle-class family, and I wanted to be independent.

I graduated in Computer Science in 2009, but I only started working in 2016, in Dubai, as a post-contract coordinator in a landscaping company. I coordinated 30+ projects with clients, vendors and teams.
People around me questioned why a woman should work. I did not oppose anyone. I explained why a career matters for women, and they came to understand it.

In Dubai, I saw how much was automated. I saw a car park itself without the driver's help, and that is where AI first caught my attention. During COVID I watched a nine-episode YouTube series about the evolution of AI, and that made me serious about it. The Avengers films also inspired me.

I came back to India in June 2019 and used the next period to settle. In 2021 I began an online AI and ML program with Purdue University. About ten months into it, in 2022, that learning got me my first developer job as a junior Python developer, and I completed the program in 2022 while working.

I have reached this point about a decade later than many people, but I'm happy, and I see everything as an opportunity. Today I'm a Product Engineer building production software, and I want to grow into an AI engineer.

superpower.title: Turning ambiguous problems into safe, shipped systems
superpower.short: My number one superpower is turning an ambiguous problem into a safe system that actually ships. I break the work into clear parts, plan it, and execute it on time. For example, I led a large user migration that had to finish in a two-day cutover window without losing any data.

story.situation: A client's legacy website had to be migrated to a modern architecture. More than 20,000 users had to be registered in Keycloak within a two-day cutover, and none of them could receive an email until the whole migration was complete.
what_i_did: I broke the migration API into three parts.
First, I registered users in Postgres, because the Keycloak reference is not the primary key.
Second, I registered them in Keycloak through a subprocess, which I later replaced with Keycloak's partial import API.
Third, I stored the emails separately, and at the client's request I built a cloud scheduler to send them later.
I ran the migration in batches of 5,000 users.
result: Registering users in Keycloak dropped from about 4 hours per 1,000 users to about 15 minutes per 1,000 users.
The whole run, including database updates and email logs, took about 8 to 10 hours.
We completed the cutover within the two-day window with zero data loss.
With the client's approval, sending the emails took three days because the email provider allows only 10,000 emails per day.

growth_areas.short: First, evaluation and observability for production AI agents, because you cannot trust an agent you cannot measure. Second, cost-aware AI design, using AI only where it pays off. Third, leadership and mentoring, so more teams can build production-grade agents that help people and do not harm them.

items.area: Evaluation and observability for production agents
items.why: An agent you cannot measure is an agent you cannot trust. In my MediBot project I built an evaluation pipeline with RAGAS, LangSmith tracing and a labeled question set, and it showed me how often an answer that looks fine is quietly wrong. I want to go deeper so problems are caught before they harm users.
items.note: She called this the most important one.

items.why: AI costs can grow so high that only a few people can use it, and some companies have been hurt by the bills. I want to use AI only where it pays off and keep cost low.

AI was created to help people have less pressure, more productive time and better work-life balance. But one small mistake can cause heavy loss of data, jobs or trust. I want to help teams build production-grade agents safely, without harming people.

I replay situations that went badly and think about how a different tone would have helped.
I don't hesitate to say sorry when I'm wrong.

failure_and_lesson.what_happened: During the testing phase of a data migration, some data was deleted and we could not find who did it. It was not in production at that time.
what_i_changed: We started backups every 24 hours, so any loss would be minimal.
We wrote production notes on what went wrong on our side and the client's side, and what not to do.
I told the client about it openly.

projects.name: MediBot
projects.type: Bootcamp project (Codebasics AI Engineering Bootcamp), not a production system
projects.stack: Python, FastAPI, Qdrant, Groq, RAGAS, LangSmith, Next.js
projects.brief: A healthcare knowledge assistant for five staff roles. Role-based access is enforced inside the vector database queries, so restricted content never reaches the LLM. It has hybrid retrieval, reranking, fail-closed guardrails, and an evaluation pipeline (RAGAS, LLM judge, 28-question labeled set).
projects.summary: A healthcare knowledge assistant for five staff roles. Access control is enforced inside Qdrant queries with role metadata filters, so restricted content never reaches the LLM, and I tested it with adversarial prompts such as role-override attempts. It uses hierarchical chunking, hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and SQL RAG. It has fail-closed input and output guardrails and an evaluation pipeline with RAGAS metrics, an LLM judge, and heuristic checks over a 28-question labeled set.

projects.name: InsightForge AI
projects.type: Bootcamp project (Codebasics AI Engineering Bootcamp), not a production system
projects.stack: Python, DeepAgents, LangGraph, FastAPI, Qdrant, Docling, APScheduler, Next.js
projects.brief: A multi-agent market-research platform. A planner splits a brief into parallel sub-tasks for isolated subagents, orchestrated by a LangGraph state machine through synthesis, writing and fact-checking. It passes references instead of full text between agents to stay within a token budget, and scores source credibility.
projects.summary: A market-intelligence research platform. A planner agent splits a brief into parallel sub-tasks run by isolated web-search, document-reader and entity-extractor subagents, orchestrated by a LangGraph state machine through synthesis, writing and fact-checking. Raw sources sit in a keyed scratch store, and agents pass references instead of full text to stay within a token budget. It adds source credibility scoring, cited reports with confidence labels, a fact-checker, and scheduled monitoring that alerts only on genuinely new findings.
